items.title: 27.3.2 Role of Inhibitors in Enzyme-Catalysed Reactions

source_refs.note: Topic 27.3.2 with the cobra box and the first Quick Check 27.3, answered (PDF 168-169); Figures 27.8 and 27.9 are redrawn in the topic 27.3 figure. Printed slips are corrected in a warning; the book's equating of non-competitive with irreversible is reported as the book's. Answers need review.

blocks.text: Small molecules or ions that cause enzymes to lose their catalytic activity are inhibitors. Different inhibitors act differently, but all stop the active site from binding the substrate.

blocks.alt: Top: an enzyme shaped like a bowl with a notched active site, a substrate of matching shape fitting into it to form an enzyme-substrate complex, and then the unchanged enzyme with two product molecules. Bottom left: a competitive inhibitor of the same shape sits in the active site, so the substrate cannot enter. Bottom right: a non-competitive inhibitor binds elsewhere on the enzyme and distorts the active site.
blocks.caption: The lock and key model and the action of inhibitors (original diagram after Figures 27.7 to 27.9).
blocks.long_description: The substrate fits the active site like a key in a lock, forms a short-lived complex and leaves as products, so one enzyme molecule can act many times. A competitive inhibitor looks like the substrate and blocks the site; a non-competitive inhibitor changes the site's shape from another position.

items: Competitive (reversible) inhibitors have the same shape as the substrate. The substrate and the inhibitor compete for the active site; the more inhibitor, the more the enzyme is deactivated for its substrate. For example, butanedioate (succinate, -OOC-CH2-CH2-COO-) is oxidised by the enzyme succinate dehydrogenase, and propanedioate (malonate, -OOC-CH2-COO-) inhibits this enzyme because it resembles succinate.

Non-competitive (irreversible) inhibitors are small ions or molecules that change the shape of the active site so that it is no longer available to the substrate. An enzyme to which an irreversible inhibitor, such as a poison, an antibiotic, an anti-metabolite or some drugs, is attached loses its activity permanently; such inhibition can cause severe health problems or even death. Penicillin is an irreversible inhibitor of the enzyme transpeptidase, which bacteria need to build their cell walls, so penicillin kills bacteria by disrupting cell wall synthesis.

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: Cobra venom contains the enzyme PLA2, which can break down the membranes of red blood cells, causing haemolysis, swelling of the affected organ and ultimately death.
